nameStory: Watershield gets its name from its floating leaves that create a natural "shield" on the water's surface. The leaves are shaped like tiny umbrellas or shields, protecting the underwater parts of the plant beneath them.
description: Watershield is a perennial aquatic plant that floats gracefully on the surface of ponds and slow-moving waters. Its bright green, oval leaves float like lily pads, attached to long stems that stretch down to roots anchored in the muddy bottom. The plant produces small purple flowers from summer into early fall, but what really sets it apart is the thick, jelly-like coating that covers all its underwater parts. This slimy mucilage makes the stems and leaf undersides feel distinctly slippery to the touch.

idTips.label: Mucilage Coating
idTips.description: All underwater parts feel incredibly slimy and slippery due to a thick, clear jelly-like coating - this is the plant's signature feature that no other New England aquatic plant shares

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Bright green, oval floating leaves that are attached to their stems at the center (like an umbrella), not at the edge like water lilies

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small purple flowers about the size of a dime that rise just above the water surface on individual stalks from June through September

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms loose colonies of floating leaves connected by slippery underwater stems, often found in shallow areas 1-6 feet deep

idTips.label: Leaf Underside
idTips.description: Flip a leaf over to reveal a reddish-purple underside covered in that distinctive slippery mucilage coating

habitat: Watershield thrives in shallow, quiet waters of ponds, lakes, and beaver ponds throughout New England, particularly those with slightly acidic water. Look for it in protected coves and backwater areas where there's little current, often growing alongside other aquatic plants like water lilies and pondweeds. It prefers muddy or sandy bottoms in water depths ranging from just a few inches to about 6 feet deep.

seasonality.spring: Young leaves begin emerging and unfurling at the surface as water warms, with the characteristic slimy coating already well-developed on all underwater parts.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full leaf coverage and small purple flowers blooming from June onward, making this the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue into September, then leaves begin to yellow and sink as temperatures drop and the plant prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground rhizomes, leaving no visible trace above water until spring returns.

funFact: Watershield's slimy coating is so effective at deterring hungry snails and other plant-eaters that some researchers think it could inspire new natural pest control methods - it's like the plant created its own slippery force field!
confusionNotes: Watershield's floating leaves might be mistaken for small water lily pads, but watershield leaves are attached at the center like tiny umbrellas, while water lily leaves are attached at a slit along one edge. Memory trick: watershield leaves look like little green umbrellas you could hold by their stems.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called watershield, this plant is actually more closely related to fanworts than to true water lilies, even though it looks more lily-like. The thick mucilage coating has made it a traditional food source in some Asian cultures, where the young leaves and shoots are harvested and prepared as a delicacy.
compareHints: Watershield is the only species in its genus Brasenia worldwide, making it truly unique. Within its family (Cabombaceae), it's most similar to fanworts (Cabomba species), but fanworts have feathery, divided underwater leaves rather than the simple floating leaves of watershield. The slimy mucilage coating is watershield's exclusive trademark that no other aquatic plant in New England possesses.
